content: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most prevalent X-linked neuromuscular disorder. As boys with DMD progress into their second decade of life, they typically lose the ability to walk and become reliant on wheelchairs for mobility. In the management of DMD, standing devices and orthoses are widely regarded as critical therapeutic tools. Clinical insights and research from other neurological conditions suggest potential benefits of using standing devices. However, the specific effects of these devices in individuals with DMD remain unclear. A comprehensive review of the evidence regarding the use of standing devices and orthoses is essential to provide guidance for individuals with DMD, healthcare professionals, policymakers, and funding bodies, as well as to inform future research directions. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of standing devices and orthoses on musculoskeletal impairments in boys and men with DMD. These impairments include issues such as pain, contractures, scoliosis development, and reduced bone density. Additionally, the review aimed to assess the secondary effects of these devices on quality of life, participation in daily activities, and patient satisfaction. The review also sought to identify any adverse events associated with the use of standing devices. To achieve these objectives, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, AMED, PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus, PEDro, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global, up to September 5, 2019. References from identified trials were examined, journal abstracts were manually searched, and trial registries were reviewed to ensure thorough coverage. The inclusion criteria for this review specified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that evaluated any model of standing device used in individuals with DMD. Control groups could include those receiving no standing device, a different model of standing device, standard care, or an alternative form of assistive weight-bearing intervention. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. Despite identifying 13 potentially relevant studies, none of these met the inclusion criteria for the review. Consequently, no RCTs or quasi-RCTs were available to assess the effectiveness of standing devices in individuals with DMD. The authors concluded that there is currently no high-quality evidence from RCTs or quasi-RCTs to determine the effectiveness of standing devices in the DMD population. This highlights the urgent need for well-designed studies to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of standing devices in this group.
